1	# The library
2	
3	The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:
4	
5	- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
6	- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
7	- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
8	- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.
9	
10	## How loops and reductions call the library
11	
12	The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:
13	
14	- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
15	- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
16	- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.
17	
18	These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.
19	
20	## The curator's decisions on the library
21	
22	- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
23	- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
24	- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
25	- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. If the generators and the body do not fix the element type, write it, also where a declared type receives the value: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` that no declared type directs gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716).
26	- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.
27	
28	## Designing a change
29	
30	- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
31	- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
32	- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
33	- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
34	- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
35	- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
36	- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
37	- A new native is a Java class under `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"), so it is an edit of walk's Java too.
38	- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.
39	
40	## Editing
41	
42	A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.
43

1	# The specification
2	
3	Three folders hold the team's specification:
4	
5	- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
6	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
7	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
8	
9	Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.
10	
11	A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.
12	
13	The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.
14	
15	To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".
16	
17	## Changing the text: the revision form
18	
19	Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.
20	
21	1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
22	   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
23	   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
24	   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
25	   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.
26	
27	   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
28	
29	2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:
30	
31	       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}
32	
33	   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.
34	
35	3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.
36	
37	4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.
38	
39	If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.
40	
41	Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.
42	
43	## Building it
44	
45	To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):
46	
47	    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
48	
49	- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'Reference .* undefined\|multiply defined\|Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
50	- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
51	- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
52	- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.
53	
54	## When the text and an implementation disagree
55	
56	- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
57	- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
58	- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.
59	
60	## Citing it
61	
62	- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
63	- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.
64

1	# The gate
2	
3	The gate runs the seven steps below on one tree, in about 25 minutes. It is green if every step passes, and red if one fails. If a step fails, run the rest, so that the summary holds every step's result.
4	
5	## What it writes
6	
7	The summary, `summary.txt`, has one tab-separated row for each suite: `track/suite`, tests, failures, errors, skipped. Below the rows, lines that start with `#` give each log's `BUILD` and `Total time:` lines, the machine that ran the gate (`# machine`), the atomic runs and the ladder's comparison. A landed summary can also end with `# microgpt-walk` lines: the `VERDICT:` and `rc=` lines of the microGPT walk check (`interpreter.md`, "The model program"), run on the landed tree. Add them only if your brief asks for the microGPT walk check on the landed tree.
8	
9	If your brief asks you to land a gate's results, put them in a new `gate/` folder in `explorations/compile-ladder/`, under the `climb-batch-` name that your brief gives, in the form of the newest one: `summary.txt`, and in `ladder/` the files `ladder.tsv`, `microgpt-phase.md`, `comparison.txt` and `microgpt-comparison.txt`. The next gate compares with the newest summary there or in `explorations/compile-ladder/gate-baseline/`, and finds no other. Land them in a commit that changes nothing else that the gate reads.
10	
11	Steps 5 and 7 use shell functions that `explorations/coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh` defines. The file runs nothing. In each Bash call of steps 5 and 7, set up the call as `build-and-caches.md` says, which sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the tree's root. Then source the file, from the root:
12	
13	    source explorations/coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh
14	
15	## When to run it
16	
17	Your brief says whether you run the gate. If it does not ask, run only your own tests (`tests-running.md`).
18	
19	If it asks, first check whether the newest gate still holds for your tree. A gate's tables stay valid until the tree changes under `ProjectFortress/` or `Library/`, or in `build.xml`, outside the test files. A test file is a `.fss`, `.fsi` or `.test` file directly in `ProjectFortress/tests/` or a `ProjectFortress/*_tests/` directory. The commit that landed the newest summary changed nothing that the gate reads. Commit your tree, then run this command. It prints each path, test files excepted, changed since that commit:
20	
21	    G=$(git log -1 --format=%H -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt')
22	    git diff --name-only $G HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library build.xml \
23	        | grep -v -E '^ProjectFortress/([^/]*_)?tests/[^/]*\.(fss|fsi|test)$'
24	
25	- If it prints a path, run the gate.
26	- If not, the newest gate holds. Run only the changed test files, through `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` (`tests-running.md`).
27	
28	## The steps
29	
30	Run these steps from the tree's root. Keep the logs of steps 2 and 4 in `tmp/gate/`, as `compileAll.txt`, `testFast.txt`, `testSystem.txt` and `testSpecData.txt`.
31	
32	1. Read the Avail column of `df -h /`. Warning: deleting `/tmp/fortress*rats` can break other live runs. If the column shows less than 1 GB, delete `/tmp/fortress*rats`, `ProjectFortress/test-tmp` and `ProjectFortress/test-caches`, and read it again. If it still shows less than 500 MB, stop and report.
33	2. Run `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS tmp/gate && mkdir -p tmp/gate`, then `ant compileAll`.
34	3. If the build printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, run the library order (`build-and-caches.md`). If not, and a source of the compiler's library changed since the caches were filled, take its step in `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library". Then copy the caches twice for the ladder regression, before anything else compiles into them:
35	
36	       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; mkdir -p $D/root
37	       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/ladder-caches
38	       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/pristine
39	
40	4. Run `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`, then `ant testSpecData`. All three must have zero failures.
41	5. Write the summary: `gate_summary tmp/gate tmp/gate/summary.txt`. Compare it: `gate_compare "$(last_landed_summary)" tmp/gate/summary.txt`. It prints a line for a suite with failures or errors, a suite with no tests, a suite whose count of tests fell, and a suite that is gone. Each such line makes the gate red. A count that rose prints nothing.
42	6. Do the atomic runs, and append their lines to the summary.
43	7. Do the ladder regression.
44	
45	## The atomic runs
46	
47	The atomic runs compile fourteen programs, and run each one three times at four threads, in about a minute. They need the library's jars in the tree's caches (`build-and-caches.md`). Run them from `ProjectFortress/`:
48	
49	    for p in AtomicTopLevelObjectVar AtomicTopLevelVar MutableTopLevelVarInLoop FirstLoadThreadsRungG \
50	             atomic0 atomic1 atomic2 atomic3 atomic4 atomic5 atomic6 \
51	             nestedTransactions0 nestedTransactions1 nestedTransactions2 ; do
52	      d=other_compiler_tests ; [ -f compiler_tests/$p.fss ] && d=compiler_tests
53	      timeout -k 5 300 ../bin/fortress compile $d/$p.fss >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "# atomic $p COMPILE-FAILED" ; continue ; }
54	      for i in 1 2 3 ; do
55	        out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$?
56	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && { out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$? ; }
57	        case "$out" in *FAIL*) r=FAIL ;; *PASS*) r=PASS ;; *) r="NO-PASS rc=$rc" ;; esac
58	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && r=TIMEOUT-TWICE
59	        echo "# atomic $p run$i threads=4 $r"
60	      done
61	    done
62	
63	The gate is red on any FAIL, NO-PASS, COMPILE-FAILED or TIMEOUT-TWICE.
64	
65	## The ladder regression
66	
67	The compile ladder records how far each test program gets through the compiler's phases, in order: parse, disambiguate, typecheck, codegen, link, run and pass. The ladder regression runs part of it again, and compares the result with the baseline, `explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/`:
68	
69	- It compiles and runs the 85 programs of the baseline's `pass-list.txt`. It compares each one's phase and output with the baseline's `raw/`.
70	- It compiles the eighteen components of the two microGPT programs, and never runs them. It compares each one's phase with the baseline's `microgpt-phase.md`.
71	
72	A file that moved gets a mark:
73	
74	- DOWN: a phase lower than the record.
75	- MISSING: a file with no output.
76	- STDOUT: output that differs from the record after the `Operation took <n>ms` line is masked.
77	- UP: a phase higher than the record. This is progress, not red.
78	
79	DOWN, MISSING and STDOUT are red, unless your brief declared that move as expected before the gate ran.
80	Warning: do not run `run-ladder.sh`, the driver over every test program, with its defaults. Its default root is shared, its cache pruning corrupts a parallel run, and its default `OUT` is a tracked folder.
81	
82	To run it, as step 7, with step 3's copies of the caches:
83	
84	1. Copy the drivers into `tmp/gate/ladder/`, and point their outputs and caches there:
85	
86	       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; B=explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19
87	       cp explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh \
88	          $B/classify.py $B/microgpt-phase.sh $B/microgpt-phase.py $D/
89	       sed -i -e "s|^OUT=.*|OUT=$D|" -e "s|^LADDER_ROOT=.*|LADDER_ROOT=$D/root|" $D/run-subset.sh
90	       sed -i -e "s|/home/user/fortress|$PWD|g" \
91	           -e "s|^export LADDER_CACHES=.*|export LADDER_CACHES=$D/root/ladder-caches|" \
92	           -e "s|^export LADDER_TMP=.*|export LADDER_TMP=$D/root/ladder-tmp|" \
93	           -e "s|^RAW=.*|RAW=$D/raw/microgpt|" -e "s|^TSV=.*|TSV=$D/microgpt-results.tsv|" $D/microgpt-phase.sh
94	       tail -n +2 $B/pass-list.txt | cut -f1 | sed 's|/|\t|' > $D/subset.txt
95	
96	2. Run the four scripts, with no arguments, in this order: `bash $D/run-subset.sh`, `python3 $D/classify.py`, `bash $D/microgpt-phase.sh` and `python3 $D/microgpt-phase.py`. Each reads and writes in `$D`. This takes about 200 s for the 85 and 35 s for the eighteen, so run them in the background (`session.md`, "Long commands"). With step 3's copies, the driver skips the library's build (about 145 s).
97	3. Compare: `ladder_compare $B $D`, then `diff <(mg_phases $B/microgpt-phase.md) <(mg_phases $D/microgpt-phase.md)`. Append each line that they print to the summary, with `# ladder ` before it.
98	
99	If your brief asks for your change's own ladder subset, write your own `subset.txt`. Put in it each file whose recorded first error in the baseline's `raw/` names something that your change touched. Run them after your edit only. Compare them with the newest landed `ladder.tsv`, or with the baseline's `raw/` for a file that the gate does not run.
100	
101	## Comparing with an earlier run
102	
103	- `ant testSystem` runs in four shards, the summary's rows `system-0` to `system-3`. A shard takes the files by their place in a sorted list, so an added file moves every later file to another shard. When you compare by hand, compare only the sum of the four. `gate_compare` sums them.
104	- In printed output, mask only these differences: the `Operation took <n>ms` line, a Java line number in a stack frame, an object's identity hash (`@` and hex digits), and a position in a library file that your change moved. In your report, list each test with a masked difference, and the kinds masked in it.
105	- If your brief asks you to compare the interpreter tests with a base run, use the two scripts in `explorations/coordinator/tools/count-run/`. `count-run.sh` runs every `ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss` under walk, one JVM per test: run it once on the base commit and once after your edit. `compare-normalised.py` compares the two runs, with the last three masks above. Each script's header gives its usage.

85	
86	\section{Where Clauses}
87	\seclabel{where-clauses}
88	
89	\note{The \KWD{where} clause syntax in this section is out of date.}
90	
91	\begin{Grammar}
92	\emph{Where} &::=& \KWD{where} \{ \emph{WhereClauseList} \}\\
93	\emph{WhereClauseList} &::=& \emph{WhereClause}(\EXP{,}
94	\emph{WhereClause})$^*$ \\
95	\emph{WhereClause} &::=& \emph{Id} \emph{Extends}\\
96	&$|$& \emph{TypeAlias} \\
97	&$|$& \emph{NatConstraint} \\
98	&$|$& \emph{IntConstraint} \\
99	&$|$& \emph{BoolConstraint} \\
100	&$|$& \emph{UnitConstraint} \\
101	&$|$& \emph{TypeRef} \KWD{coerces} \emph{TypeRef}\\
102	&$|$& \emph{TypeRef} \KWD{widens} \emph{TypeRef}\\
103	\end{Grammar}
104	
105	
106	Static parameters may have constraints placed on them
107	in a \KWD{where} clause.
108	A \KWD{where} clause begins with
109	\KWD{where}, followed by a sequence of static
110	parameter constraints enclosed in braces \EXP{\{} and \EXP{\}},
111	and separated by commas.
112	
113	
114	A \KWD{where} clause may introduce new static variables, i.e., identifiers
115	for types and other static entities that may not be static parameters.
116	We use the term \emph{\KWD{where}-clause variables} to refer to
117	static variables that are not also static parameters.
118	The \KWD{where}-clause variables must be bound in a \KWD{where} clause.
119	
120	
121	A static parameter constraint is one of the following forms:
122	\begin{itemize}
123	\item a trait constraint consisting of the identifier of
124	a naked type variable, followed by \KWD{extends}
125	followed by a set of trait references which may include naked type variables,
126	\item a type alias (described in \secref{type-alias}),
127	\item an arithmetic constraint,
128	\item a boolean constraint,
129	\item a unit equality constraint,
130	\item a \KWD{coerces} constraint (described in
131	  \secref{coercion-declarations}), or
132	\item a \KWD{widens} constraint (described in
133	  \secref{coercion-declarations}).
134	\end{itemize}
135	A \KWD{where} clause may include mutually recursive constraints.
136	All static variables in a trait, object, or functional declaration must
137	occur either as a static parameter or as a \KWD{where}-clause variable.
138	\appref{where-calculus} describes a Fortress core calculus with
139	\KWD{where} clauses.
140	
141	An entry of an \KWD{extends} clause may carry a \KWD{where} clause of its
142	own (\secref{trait-decls}).
143	If that clause introduces no \KWD{where}-clause variable and all its
144	constraints are trait constraints, the declared trait or object extends the
145	entry's type exactly where the constraints hold:
146	an instance whose static arguments satisfy them is of that type,
147	and an instance whose static arguments do not satisfy them is not.
148	Within the declaration the constraints hold: its \KWD{extends} clause and
149	its members are checked as if the constraints were in the declaration's own
150	\KWD{where} clause.
151	So a list is totally ordered exactly where its elements are:
152	%trait List[\E\] extends { ZeroIndexed[\E\],
153	%    LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] } }
154	%end
155	\begin{Fortress}
156	\(\KWD{trait}\:\TYP{List}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket \KWD{extends} \{\TYP{ZeroIndexed}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket,\)\\
157	{\tt~~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \TYP{LexicographicOrder}\llbracket\TYP{List}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket,E\rrbracket \KWD{where} \{E \KWD{extends}\:\TYP{StandardTotalOrder}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket\}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
158	\(\KWD{end}\)
159	\end{Fortress}
160	\revision{revival-conditional}{This paragraph and its example are new.
161	The Working Draft of February 2011 gave each entry of an \KWD{extends}
162	clause an optional \KWD{where} clause in its grammar and stated no meaning
163	for it, and its front matter lists conditional extension among the
164	features not yet supported.}
165	
166	A \KWD{where}-clause variable may not appear as a static argument
167	in an \KWD{extends} clause.
168	Such an occurrence would make the declared trait or object a subtype of
169	one instantiation for each type that the variable may stand for,
170	which instantiation exclusion forbids
171	(\secref{trait-types} and \secref{trait-decls});
172	the second of the three declarations below shows why.
173	\revision{revival-where}{This restriction is new.
174	The three declarations that follow were offered as legal by the
175	Working Draft of February 2011; they are kept as examples of what is not
176	allowed, each with the way to write it.}
177	
178	In particular, a trait declaration may not extend other instantiations
179	of itself through a \KWD{where}-clause variable.
180	The following declaration would express that the static parameter \VAR{S}
181	of \VAR{C} is covariant, making \EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket} a subtype of
182	\EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} for every supertype \VAR{T} of \VAR{S};
183	it is not allowed:
184	%(* Not allowed! *)
185	%trait C[\S\] extends C[\T\]
186	%  where {S extends T, T extends Object}
187	%end
188	\begin{Fortress}
189	\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
190	\(\KWD{trait} C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{extends} C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
191	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{S \KWD{extends} T, T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
192	\(\KWD{end}\)
193	\end{Fortress}
194	Static parameters are invariant:
195	\EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket} is a subtype of \EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
196	only if \VAR{S} and \VAR{T} are the same type.
197	A value of one instantiation is widened to another by a function
198	whose bounded static parameters state that one argument extends the other:
199	%trait C[\S\]
200	%  getter item(): S
201	%end
202	%object CItem[\S\](item: S) extends C[\S\] end
203	%widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\] = CItem[\T\](c.item)
204	\begin{Fortress}
205	\(\KWD{trait}\:C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket\)\\
206	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{getter}\:\VAR{item}()\COLON S\)\-\\\poptabs
207	\(\KWD{end}\)\\
208	\(\KWD{object}\:\TYP{CItem}\llbracket{}S\rrbracket(\VAR{item}\COLON S) \KWD{extends}\:C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{end}\)\\
209	\(\VAR{widen}\llbracket{}T, S \KWD{extends}\:T\rrbracket(c\COLON C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket)\COLON C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket = \TYP{CItem}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(c.\VAR{item})\)
210	\end{Fortress}
211	so that, where a trait \TYP{Dog} extends a trait \TYP{Animal} and \VAR{d}
212	is a \EXP{C\llbracket\TYP{Dog}\rrbracket},
213	\EXP{\VAR{widen}\llbracket\TYP{Animal}, \TYP{Dog}\rrbracket(d)} is a
214	\EXP{C\llbracket\TYP{Animal}\rrbracket} with the same item.
215	The library's covariant collections are written this way.
216	\revision{revival-covariance}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that
217	trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of themselves,
218	and gave the declaration above as the way to express covariance.
219	The type group's later design declares variance instead with a
220	\KWD{covariant} modifier on a static parameter
221	(the team's later Types chapter, Luchangco, 2012),
222	which is implemented on neither the interpreter nor the compiled path;
223	the revival's decision record and row~404 of its gap ledger
224	say what is known of it.}
225	
226	
227	Trait declarations need not have any static parameters in order
228	to have a \KWD{where} clause. But the following trait
229	declaration is not allowed:
230	%(* Not allowed! *)
231	%trait C extends D[\T\]
232	%  where {T extends Object}
233	%end
234	\begin{Fortress}
235	\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
236	\(\KWD{trait} C \KWD{extends} D\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
237	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
238	\(\KWD{end}\)
239	\end{Fortress}
240	In this declaration, trait \VAR{C} would be a subtrait of \emph{every}
241	instantiation of parametric trait \VAR{D}. Thus, trait \VAR{C} would have all
242	of the methods of every instantiation of \VAR{D}. By thinking of the
243	declaration this way, we can see what restrictions we need to impose on
244	the trait \VAR{C} in order for it to be sensible. If trait
245	\VAR{C} inherits a method declaration that refers to \VAR{T}, it really
246	contains infinitely many methods (one for each instantiation of \VAR{T}).
247	However, instantiations of the \KWD{where}-clause variables are not
248	explicit from the program text as static parameters are.
249	It must be possible to infer which method is referred to at the call site.
250	%%So every method invocation is annotated with static types by type inference.
251	If there is not enough information to infer which method is called,

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table was produced, 1 if it could not be. 20 s in the main tree,
# measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#
# The two sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-22 from
# explorations/perf-probes/prelude/, so that the gate does not depend on a probe
# directory: WorldFlip.java (Shell.useInterpreterLibraries() plus
# PhaseOrder.compilerPhaseOrder, both public, which is the world switch without an edit
# to a tracked file) and shadow-src/.../StaticChecker.java, a copy of
# ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java with three
# instrumentation points added: it names each compilation unit it checks and prints that
# unit's error count, and it catches the OverloadingChecker crash instead of dying on it.
# It is put AHEAD of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath, the technique of
# perf-probes/prelude/run-all.sh:33-35. A copy of a tracked source goes stale silently,
# so the checksum of the tracked one is recorded here and the table's "#shadow" line
# says whether it still matches.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false, read
# at OverloadingChecker.scala:77), since 2026-09-27 (climb batch 7). The memo is keyed on
# declaration pairs and hides 27 to 35 errors depending on the build order once an api's
# overloading check runs (perf-probes/nat/triage.md section 1; FACTS.md, "The hidden
# layer, classified"); with it off every build gives one count. The table's "#cache"
# row says so. On the tree of 2026-09-27 the count is 62 with the memo on and off,
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:              15           0          11           0           3          14
Swap:              0           0           0
 02:20:53 up  1:57,  0 user,  load average: 0.19, 1.51, 3.01
4

01:01:37  cd /home/user/fortress-condextend && P="Library/FortressLibrary.fsi Library/FortressLibrary.fss Library/List.fsi Library/List.fss Library/PureList.fss ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TypeWellFormedChecker.scala ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Decls.scala ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/staticenv/KindEnv.scala ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala"; git add -- $P && git commit -q -m "Conditional extension in the compiled checker, and the list order under it

A trait or object that extends a type under a where clause of trait
constraints only is that type exactly where the constraints hold: parents
leaves such an entry out, conditionalParents gives it with its conditions
at the type's static arguments, and the subtype case of a trait type counts
it where they hold, as a formula (beside rung A's reading of a parent that
opens, which it keeps). KindEnv.withExtendsConditions adds the conditions to
the declaration's where clause, so that its members and its extends clause
are checked with them holding (Decls' and TypeWellFormedChecker's trait and
object cases). From the where-clause probe's B.3, re-based onto climb batch
17.

The library: LexicographicOrder's element bounded by StandardTotalOrder;
List (and PureList's List) extends LexicographicOrder under that condition,
with ZeroIndexed written outside it; a structural = kept on List with
LexicographicOrder's body, so that a list of unordered elements keeps its
equality; the team's comment 'a hack to avoid the error of overloaded
methods' removed above the generic distribute it no longer describes.

Edits the original tree: TypeAnalyzer.scala, KindEnv.scala, Decls.scala,
TypeWellFormedChecker.scala, FortressLibrary.fsi/.fss, List.fsi/.fss,
PureList.fss.

+(* A pair is ordered when its elements are, and a vector adds when its elements do: a conditional extension holds where its condition does, and the declaration's members are checked with the condition holding. *)
+component CondExtendChecker
+export Executable
+
+trait Ord[\T extends Ord[\T\]\]
+  lt(o: T): Boolean
+end
+trait Add[\T extends Add[\T\]\]
+  plus(o: T): T
+end
+object Num(v: ZZ32) extends { Ord[\Num\], Add[\Num\] }
+  lt(o: Num): Boolean = v < o.v
+  plus(o: Num): Num = Num(v + o.v)
+end
+object Str(s: String) extends Ord[\Str\]
+  lt(o: Str): Boolean = false
+end
+object Lst[\E\](a: E, b: E) extends { Ord[\Lst[\E\]\] where { E extends Ord[\E\] } }
+  lt(o: Lst[\E\]): Boolean = a.lt(o.a)
+end
+object Vec[\E\](x: E) extends { Add[\Vec[\E\]\] where { E extends Add[\E\] } }
+  plus(o: Vec[\E\]): Vec[\E\] = Vec[\E\](x.plus(o.x))
+end
+
+less[\T extends Ord[\T\]\](x: T, y: T): Boolean = x.lt(y)
+sum[\T extends Add[\T\]\](x: T, y: T): T = x.plus(y)
+
+run(): () = do
+    println(less(Lst[\Num\](Num(1), Num(2)), Lst[\Num\](Num(2), Num(1))))
+    println(less(Lst[\Str\](Str("a"), Str("b")), Lst[\Str\](Str("b"), Str("a"))))
+    w: Vec[\Num\] = sum(Vec[\Num\](Num(1)), Vec[\Num\](Num(2)))
+    println("PASS")
+  end
+
+end

+\subsection{Conditional extension}
+\seclabel{revival-conditional}
+
+\begin{description}
+\item[Affected section] \secref{where-clauses}.
+\item[Change] A paragraph and an example are added, with a box: where the
+\KWD{where} clause of an entry of an \KWD{extends} clause introduces no
+\KWD{where}-clause variable and all its constraints are trait constraints,
+the declared trait or object extends the entry's type exactly where the
+constraints hold, and within the declaration the constraints hold while its
+\KWD{extends} clause and its members are checked; the example is
+\library's list, totally ordered exactly where its elements are.
+\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival
+decided on 16~October 2026 to build the forms of \KWD{where} clause the team
+wrote down, among them that a trait that extends another under a
+\KWD{where} condition is that type only where the condition holds and that
+its members are checked under the condition, as Haskell checks an
+instance's context, Rust a conditional implementation and Swift a
+conditional conformance.
+The grammar gives each entry of an \KWD{extends} clause its own optional
+\KWD{where} clause, and the text orders lists ``whose elements support these
+same comparison operators''
+(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex},
+lines 284--285), which no
+unconditional declaration of the list type can state:
+\library\ declared their list type as lexicographically ordered at every
+element type, so the compiled type checker refused the comparison of two
+elements of an unbounded type in the order's own body.
+The team's internal notes foresaw conditional subtyping and its cost,
+that ``we may also not be able to tell whether a trait has a particular
+method'' (\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/internal-document.tex},
+lines 538--543, in its subsection ``No Wrapped Fields Whose Types Are Naked
+Type Variables'').
+A clause that introduces a \KWD{where}-clause variable, or whose
+constraints are not all trait constraints, keeps the reading it had: the
+entry is extended at every instance.
+\library's list keeps an element-wise \EXP{=} of its own outside the
+condition, so that a list whose elements are not ordered, a list of pairs
+among them, is still compared element by element.
+The alternative not taken is to read the clause as limiting nothing, the
+extension holding at every instance, under which the clause has no effect
+and the list's order needs another construct.
+The full reasoning is in
+\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-conditional-extension/REPORT.md}
+in the revival's repository.
+\item[Effect] The compiled type checker reads such a clause as this
+section says: a value of an instance whose static arguments satisfy the
+constraints is of the entry's type, one whose static arguments do not is
+refused where that type is expected, and the declaration's members and
+\KWD{extends} clause are checked with the constraints holding.
+\library's \TYP{LexicographicOrder} bounds its element type by
+\TYP{StandardTotalOrder}, and its list extends it under the constraint
+that its element type does, so the compiled type checker orders a list
+exactly where its elements are totally ordered.
+It gives no order to a list of partially ordered elements, of \TYP{RR64},
+\TYP{QQ} or ranges among them, where \secref{partial-total-orders} says
+that a lexicographic order ``may be partial or total depending on whether the
+ordering of the elements is partial or total''
+(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex},
+lines 520--522): no partial lexicographic order of lists is declared.
+The compiled type checker still lets a member that it checked with the
+constraints holding be called where they fail: it accepts a call of such
+a member on an instance whose static arguments do not satisfy them
+(row~NEW-X-1 of the revival's gap ledger).
+Its other readers of an \KWD{extends} clause, the members a type inherits
+and its checks of the type hierarchy, read the entry as extended at every
+instance.
+The interpreter reads the extension as holding at every instance, and so
+does the compiled run time: a type test of an instance whose static
+arguments fail the constraints answers \VAR{true} on both
+(row~NEW-X-2, gated for the interpreter by
+\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/XXXConditionalExtensionTypeTestWalk.fss}),
+so the interpreter keeps the order of a list of tuples or of floating-point
+numbers.
+The code generator compiles a declaration whose \KWD{extends} clause has
+such a clause; it refuses one that carries a \KWD{where} clause of its own
+(row~701).
+\item[Original text] No such paragraph. The grammar is unchanged:
+\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, line 83,
+\begin{quote}
+\emph{TraitTypeWhere} ::= \emph{TraitType} \emph{Where}?
+\end{quote}
+and the front matter lists ``where clauses and conditional extension''
+among the features not yet supported
+(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress/preamble.tex}, line 82).
+\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
+\end{description}
+
 \subsection{The covariance example}
 \seclabel{revival-covariance}

component conditionalExtension

export Executable

trait PartialOrderAndBoundedLattice[\T, opr LEOPR, opr MINOPR, opr MAXOPR\] end
trait Identity[\opr PLUS\] end

trait RationalQuantity[\unit U absorbs unit, bool ninf, bool lt, bool eq,
                        bool gt, bool pinf, bool nan\]
    extends {
      RationalQuantity[\U, ninf', lt', eq', gt', pinf', nan'\]
              where [\bool ninf', bool lt', bool eq', bool gt', bool pinf',
                      bool nan' \]
                    { ninf IMPLIES ninf', lt IMPLIES lt',
                      eq IMPLIES eq', gt IMPLIES gt', pinf IMPLIES pinf',
                      nan IMPLIES nan'
                    },
              PartialOrderAndBoundedLattice[\RationalQuantity[\U, ninf, lt, eq, gt, pinf, nan\], <=, MIN, MAX\]
              where { ninf AND pinf AND NOT nan }
            }
    where { ninf OR lt OR eq OR gt OR pinf OR nan }
  coerce(x: Identity[\+\]) = 0
end

run() = println "Conditional extension with where clauses can be parsed."

end

#!/bin/bash
# old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...
#
# Runs the old code, the base's: bin/fortress of the batch's one base build, with FORTRESS_HOME set to the
# base build and FORTRESS_CACHES to a private caches folder. If the folder does not exist yet, it is first
# made as a copy of the base build's default_repository/caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). The paths in those caches
# are the base build's own, so nothing is translated, and no worktree is made.
#
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss    the compiled path: compile ...
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P            ... then run
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss            walk
#
# Every cache a run writes goes to the private folder: every cache directory and the logs are under
# fortress.caches (repository/ProjectProperties.java:283-299), which FORTRESS_CACHES sets, and
# bin/fortress_classpath and bin/run_classpath put FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache on the class path.
# Under the base build a run reads the build, the library sources and default_repository/configuration, and
# writes nothing that stays: the parser writes its error logs beside each file it parses from source and
# deletes them (compiler/Parser.java:349-367), so a compile of a program that exports Executable creates and
# deletes two empty, gitignored logs beside Library/Executable.fsi. Two runs at once may share those two
# names; that is harmless, because the base's library parses without errors, so both logs stay empty and
# a log removed by the other run reads as empty (Parser.java:373-377). Measured in
# explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md, section 6.
#
# Keep the private folder and your programs outside the base build (the program's own logs go beside it).
# Refuses (exit 2) a base build that is not built, and a private folder inside the base build.
set -euo pipefail
USAGE='usage: old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...'
BASE=$(realpath "${1:?$USAGE}")
PRIV_ARG=${2:?$USAGE}
shift 2
[ -x "$BASE/bin/fortress" ] && [ -e "$BASE/ProjectFortress/build/com/sun/fortress/Shell.class" ] \
  && [ -e "$BASE/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar" ] \
  || { echo "old-fortress: $BASE is not a built tree" >&2 ; exit 2 ; }
PRIV=$(realpath -m "$PRIV_ARG")
case "$PRIV/" in "$BASE"/*) echo "old-fortress: $PRIV is inside the base build $BASE" >&2 ; exit 2 ;; esac
if [ ! -d "$PRIV" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$PRIV")"
    PART="$PRIV.part.$$"
    cp -a "$BASE/default_repository/caches" "$PART"
    mv -T "$PART" "$PRIV" 2>/dev/null || rm -rf "$PART"     # another run made it first: use that one

component CondAccept
export Executable

trait Ord[\T extends Ord[\T\]\]
  lt(o: T): Boolean
end
trait Shows
  show(): String
end
object Num(v: ZZ32) extends { Ord[\Num\], Shows }
  lt(o: Num): Boolean = v < o.v
  show(): String = "n"
end
object Lst[\E\](a: E, b: E) extends { Ord[\Lst[\E\]\] where { E extends Ord[\E\] } }
  lt(o: Lst[\E\]): Boolean = a.lt(o.a)
  (* self is ordered inside, where the condition holds *)
  lt2(o: Lst[\E\]): Boolean = less(self, o)
end
(* two constraints in one clause *)
object Two[\E\](a: E) extends { Ord[\Two[\E\]\] where { E extends Ord[\E\], E extends Shows } }
  lt(o: Two[\E\]): Boolean = a.lt(o.a)
end
(* a trait extends conditionally, an object extends the trait *)
trait L[\E\] extends { Ord[\L[\E\]\] where { E extends Ord[\E\] } }
  getter hd(): E
  lt(o: L[\E\]): Boolean = hd.lt(o.hd)
end
object C[\E\](h: E) extends L[\E\]
  getter hd(): E = h
end
(* a condition on the second of two parameters *)
object Pr[\A, B\](a: A, b: B) extends { Ord[\Pr[\A,B\]\] where { B extends Ord[\B\] } }
  lt(o: Pr[\A,B\]): Boolean = b.lt(o.b)
end

less[\T extends Ord[\T\]\](x: T, y: T): Boolean = x.lt(y)
viaBound[\T extends Ord[\T\]\](x: Lst[\T\], y: Lst[\T\]): Boolean = less(x, y)
useOrd(x: Ord[\Lst[\Num\]\]): Boolean = x.lt(x)

run(): () = do
  n1 = Num(1)
  n2 = Num(2)
  println(less(Lst[\Num\](n1, n2), Lst[\Num\](n2, n1)))
  println(less(Lst(n2, n1), Lst(n1, n2)))
  println(viaBound(Lst[\Num\](n1, n1), Lst[\Num\](n2, n2)))
  println(useOrd(Lst[\Num\](n1, n2)))
  println(Lst[\Num\](n1, n2).lt2(Lst[\Num\](n2, n1)))
  println(less(Lst[\Lst[\Num\]\](Lst[\Num\](n1, n1), Lst[\Num\](n1, n1)), Lst[\Lst[\Num\]\](Lst[\Num\](n2, n2), Lst[\Num\](n2, n2))))
  println(less(Two[\Num\](n1), Two[\Num\](n2)))
  println(less[\L[\Num\]\](C[\Num\](n2), C[\Num\](n1)))
  println(less(Pr[\String, Num\]("x", n1), Pr[\String, Num\]("y", n2)))
  println("PASS")
end

end
EOF

  lt(o: T): Boolean

The code generator asks its analyzer, which binds no declaration's static
parameters, whether a type that inherits a method through a conditional
parent is below that parent (STypesUtil.removeIdenticallyCoveredMethods,
from CodeGen's constructor). With conditional parents read, the condition
E extends B asked for E's bound, and the compile died with a CompilerBug,
'E is not in the kind env [][]', for a program the base compiles. A
condition on a type variable the analyzer's kind environment does not bind
is now read as holding, so such an analyzer reads the parent at every
instance, as the code generator builds the class; an analyzer that binds
the variable checks the condition as before. The read counts as a read of
the context, so no such answer is shared as a ground answer.

object inheriting lt from a trait and from its conditional parent: on the

368	An entry of an \KWD{extends} clause may carry a \KWD{where} clause of its
369	own (\secref{trait-decls}).
370	If that clause introduces no \KWD{where}-clause variable and all its
371	constraints are trait constraints, the declared trait or object extends the
372	entry's type exactly where the constraints hold:
373	an instance whose static arguments satisfy them is of that type,
374	and an instance whose static arguments do not satisfy them is not.
375	Within the declaration the constraints hold: its \KWD{extends} clause and
376	its members are checked as if the constraints were in the declaration's own
377	\KWD{where} clause.
378	So a list is totally ordered exactly where its elements are:
379	%trait List[\E\] extends { ZeroIndexed[\E\],
380	%    LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] } }
381	%end
382	\begin{Fortress}
383	\(\KWD{trait}\:\TYP{List}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket \KWD{extends} \{\TYP{ZeroIndexed}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket,\)\\
384	{\tt~~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \TYP{LexicographicOrder}\llbracket\TYP{List}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket,E\rrbracket \KWD{where} \{E \KWD{extends}\:\TYP{StandardTotalOrder}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket\}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
385	\(\KWD{end}\)
386	\end{Fortress}
387	\revision{revival-conditional}{This paragraph and its example are new.
388	The Working Draft of February 2011 gave each entry of an \KWD{extends}
389	clause an optional \KWD{where} clause in its grammar and stated no meaning
390	for it, and its front matter lists conditional extension among the
391	features not yet supported.}

160	\item[Affected section] \secref{where-clauses}.
161	\item[Change] A paragraph and an example are added, with a box: where the
162	\KWD{where} clause of an entry of an \KWD{extends} clause introduces no
163	\KWD{where}-clause variable and all its constraints are trait constraints,
164	the declared trait or object extends the entry's type exactly where the
165	constraints hold, and within the declaration the constraints hold while its
166	\KWD{extends} clause and its members are checked; the example is
167	\library's list, totally ordered exactly where its elements are.
168	\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival
169	decided on 16~October 2026 to build the forms of \KWD{where} clause the team
170	wrote down, among them that a trait that extends another under a
171	\KWD{where} condition is that type only where the condition holds and that
172	its members are checked under the condition, as Haskell checks an
173	instance's context, Rust a conditional implementation and Swift a
174	conditional conformance.
175	The grammar gives each entry of an \KWD{extends} clause its own optional
176	\KWD{where} clause, and the text orders lists ``whose elements support these
177	same comparison operators''
178	(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex},
179	lines 284--285), which no
180	unconditional declaration of the list type can state:
181	\library\ declared their list type as lexicographically ordered at every
182	element type, so the compiled type checker refused the comparison of two
183	elements of an unbounded type in the order's own body.
184	The team's internal notes foresaw conditional subtyping and its cost,
185	that ``we may also not be able to tell whether a trait has a particular
186	method'' (\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/internal-document.tex},
187	lines 538--543, in its subsection ``No Wrapped Fields Whose Types Are Naked
188	Type Variables'').
189	A clause that introduces a \KWD{where}-clause variable, or whose
190	constraints are not all trait constraints, keeps the reading it had: the
191	entry is extended at every instance.
192	\library's list keeps an element-wise \EXP{=} of its own outside the
193	condition, so that a list whose elements are not ordered, a list of pairs
194	among them, is still compared element by element.
195	The alternative not taken is to read the clause as limiting nothing, the
196	extension holding at every instance, under which the clause has no effect
197	and the list's order needs another construct.
198	The full reasoning is in
199	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-conditional-extension/REPORT.md}
200	in the revival's repository.
201	\item[Effect] The compiled type checker reads such a clause as this
202	section says: a value of an instance whose static arguments satisfy the
203	constraints is of the entry's type, one whose static arguments do not is
204	refused where that type is expected, and the declaration's members and
205	\KWD{extends} clause are checked with the constraints holding.
206	\library's \TYP{LexicographicOrder} bounds its element type by
207	\TYP{StandardTotalOrder}, and its list extends it under the constraint
208	that its element type does, so the compiled type checker orders a list
209	exactly where its elements are totally ordered.

content.content:
section says: a value of an instance whose static arguments satisfy the
constraints is of the entry's type, one whose static arguments do not is
refused where that type is expected, and the entry and the declaration's
members are checked with the constraints holding, its other entries without
them.
\library's \TYP{LexicographicOrder} bounds its element type by
\TYP{StandardTotalOrder}, and its list extends it under the constraint
that its element type does, so the compiled type checker orders a list
exactly where its elements are totally ordered.
It gives no order to a list of partially ordered elements, of \TYP{RR64},
\TYP{QQ} or ranges among them, where \secref{partial-total-orders} says
that a lexicographic order ``may be partial or total depending on whether the
ordering of the elements is partial or total''
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex},
lines 520--522), and where the operators chapter's subsection
``Comparisons Operators'' compares lists ``whose elements support these same
comparison operators'', as floating-point numbers do: no partial
lexicographic order of lists is declared.
The compiled type checker still lets a member that it checked with the
constraints holding be called where they fail: it accepts a call of such
a member on an instance whose static arguments do not satisfy them
(row~NEW-X-1 of the revival's gap ledger).
Its other readers of an \KWD{extends} clause, the members a type inherits
and its checks of the type hierarchy, read the entry as extended at every
instance.
The interpreter reads the extension as holding at every instance, and so
does the compiled run time: a type test of an instance whose static
arguments fail the constraints answers \VAR{true} on both
(row~NEW-X-2, gated for the interpreter by
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/XXXConditionalExtensionTypeTestWalk.fss}),
so the interpreter keeps the order of a list of tuples or of floating-point
numbers.
The code generator compiles a declaration whose \KWD{extends} clause has

== explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

# Rung X of climb batch 18: the skeptic's review

Rung `rung-checker-conditional-extension`, branch `wip/rung-checker-conditional-extension`, worktree `/home/user/fortress-condextend`. Head judged: `37f5f8c84` (the worker's head `706db7314` with its REPORT.md written from the run's journal, no code changed). Head after: the commit that adds this file. Base `db8fecd22`, old code from `/home/user/fortress-base18`.

Verdict: **contested**. The change is right with the fixes below; one fix (section 4.2) is contested.

## 1. What I checked

- **The tables.** I ran the count stage on the base build and on the worker's head in one session, one after the other, nothing else of mine running (nproc 4, Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz, openjdk 25.0.4.1, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, `nice -n 19`, load at start 0.16 and 0.99): `time explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh $S/base.txt $S/base` in a call set up for the base build, the same in the rung's tree. `real 1m6.347s` (base) and `real 1m7.061s` (head), against the worker's 76.4, 72.4 and 76.5 s: the same order, within the noise. My base table and normalised `run.txt` equal the worker's base run byte for byte (`cmp` silent); my head table and normalised `run.txt` equal the worker's `change` run (`a2a068aac`), so the head (`ea8b4bf36`'s code) has the same results as the change before the second pass. `diff` of my base and head tables: `< #total 31`, `< #locations 30`, `> #total 30`, `> #locations 29`; the `run.txt` files differ by the 27 lines of `FortressLibrary.fss:2063:45`, 'Could not check call to operator CMP', and by positions after `FortressLibrary.fss:3232` one line up. The distance: `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/compare.sh explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-17/gate/distance.txt tmp/rung-checker-conditional-extension/distance-postedit.txt` prints 'DISTANCE DOWN 35 -> 34 (-1)', 'class G1 1 -> 0'; site by site (kind and location of `explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv` against the worker's `dist-post/errors.tsv`) only `FortressLibrary.fss:2063` is gone; every other row moved by the edit's lines only (`:4369` to `:4368` and the like; `List.fss:140` to `:146`); none came. The report's tables hold.
- **Test first**, in the worker's transcript: the two compiled tests copied in at 00:51:01 (call `C6SsTT`), seen failing through `junit.sh` on `db8fecd22` at 00:51:25 (`N4AEsb`: 'Ill-formed type: Ord[\E\]', 'File CondExtendChecker.fss has 4 errors.', 'Saw wrong failure. compile', 'Tests run: 2,  Failures: 2'); the walk test written at 00:51:10 and run through `harness-one.sh` at 00:51:34 (`9uazq5`: 'FAIL: a Boolean: true =/= a Boolean: false', 'OK Saw expected exception'), shown red once at 00:51:54 (`uGXCRh`: 'Missing expected failure'); the first edit at 00:55:28, the first build at 00:56:26, the library edits after both; the last code edit at 01:07:31 (`SopmMg`), and the passing run after it at 01:14:59 (`QyyCfC`: 'typecheck ... CondExtendChecker  OK', 'File XXXCondExtendRefuseChecker.fss has 2 errors.', 'OK (17 tests)'). The order holds.
- **The diff** against the section, B.3 of the probe (`git -C /home/user/fortress-probe-where diff`), P-151 and the curator's reading in `explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md:30` ("the condition holds inside the declaration while its members and overrides are checked, as Swift, Rust and Haskell check it"). The port follows B.3 and keeps rung A's reading of a parent that opens; the worker's three deviations (one predicate for which entries are conditional; conditional parents in the case of a trait that opens sizes; the fast path) are sound. The memo keys: `memoParents` reads the trait table only; `pSubMemo` is per analyzer, whose kind environment is fixed; a ground answer is stored only when no context was read, and every condition on a type variable reads the context (the variable case calls `traits.readContext()`, `TypeAnalyzer.scala:174`, `:202`), and so does my fix's new read (section 4.1). No memo key misses an input.
- **The other readers** of an `extends` clause (REPORT.md section 10): each citation opened (`ExclusionOracle.scala:184-190`, `TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:92`, `:119`, `:206`, `:242`, `:288`, `:401`, `:443`, `STypesUtil.scala:1265`, `:1494-1497`, `:1687-1689`, `:1771`, `:1812`, `OverloadingChecker.scala:143-148`, `Formula.scala:609`, `Functionals.scala:434`, `:1343`, `TypeAnalyzer.scala:536-537`); each says what the report says. One reader the report does not list: the code generator's analyzer, through `STypesUtil.properlyInheritedMethodsNotIdenticallyCovered` from `CodeGen`'s constructor (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:485`), which crashed (section 4.1).
- **The report's provenance lines**, each opened: `distance-sites.tsv:13` is the `:2063` site; `opr-overview.tex:294-295` the list sentence; `KindEnv.scala:116-131` `constraintBounds`; `TypeAnalyzer.scala:291`, `:938-939`, `:956-962`, `KindEnv.scala:184-188`, `List.fss:106-107` the lines named; `changes.tex:198-200` is now `:199-201` after my contested edit's added line (section 4.2); every historical file is in `a874948ac`.
- **The specification's citations** in the new Appendix I entry, each opened in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`: `opr-overview.tex` lines 284-285, `internal-document.tex` lines 538-543 in "No Wrapped Fields Whose Types Are Naked Type Variables", `algebraic-constraints.tex` lines 520-522, `traits.tex` line 83, `preamble.tex` line 82. All hold.
- **The ledger**: `ledger-find` for conditional, LexicographicOrder, extends where, kind env and comprises where variable; rows 17, 71, 355, 634, 701, 748, 752, 756 read whole. Row 71's notes count `List.fsi`'s errors on the compiled path, which the rung's `ZeroIndexed[\E\]` moves (section 4.4). The new rows NEW-X-1 (1,016 characters, notes 599) and NEW-X-2 (936, notes 500) fit the template.
- **Competing declarations**: `condition`, `isConditional`, `conditionalParents`, `withConditionalParents`, `extendsConditions`, `withExtendsConditions` are declared once in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`; the components `CondExtendInheritedMember` and `XXXCondExtendUnconditionalEntryChecker` once in both corpora.
- **Threads**: the diff holds no mutable variable, field, `atomic` block or library state; the Scala walk's `analyzer` variable is the checker's own single-threaded pattern. No one- and four-thread runs were needed.

## 2. My programs (`tmp/rung-checker-conditional-extension/skeptic/`)

Run with `old-fortress.sh` on the base build (old) and on this tree's build with a private caches folder (new), compiled path and walk:

| program | old | new (worker's head) | new (after my fixes) |
|---|---|---|---|

| `CondInheritGen` (an unbounded `Ord`, so the old code takes the declaration), compile and run | `true`, `PASS` | `CondInheritGen.fss:10:24-25: E is not in the kind env [][]` | `true`, `PASS` |
| `CondRefuse` (an unbounded generic over `Lst[\T\]`, `Lst[\Lst[\Fn\]\]`, `Two[\Num\]` missing `Shows`), typecheck | 4 errors (the declarations') | 3 errors, the three calls | the same |
| `CondFunctional` (a functional `<` under the condition) | 1 error (`a < o.a` over `E`) | `true`, `PASS` | not rerun |
| `CondOverload`, `CondOverloadFail` (overloads on `Ord[\Lst[\X\]\]` and `Lst[\X\]`) | `lst lst PASS`; `lst PASS` | the same | `lst lst PASS` |
| `CondMember2` (a member of the object itself called where the condition fails) | 'No such method E.show.' | compiled, 'w', 'REACHED', 'NoSuchMethodError: ... FZZ32.show()'; walk 'Cannot find definition for method show given receiver 1: ZZ32' | the same (NEW-X-1, another face) |
| `CondAssign` (`s: Shows = Box[\ZZ32\](1)`) | compiles, `PASS` | 'Right-hand side has type Box[\ZZ32\], but declared type is Shows.'; walk `PASS` (NEW-X-2) | the same |
| `CondOtherEntry` (`Bad[\E\]` extends `Wrap[\E\]` beside a conditional entry, `Wrap[\T extends Ord[\T\]\]`) | 'Ill-formed type: Wrap[\E\]' | compiled; 'REACHED', 'NoSuchMethodError: ... CondOtherEntry$Fn.lt(CondOtherEntry$Fn)'; walk 'Cannot find definition for method lt given receiver Fn' | refused, 'Ill-formed type: Wrap[\E\]' (section 4.2) |
| `ListOrderWalk` (lists of integers, pairs, floats, strings, the empty list, nested lists: `<`, `CMP`, `=`), walk | `ints < true CMP LessThan = false =self true`, `pairs = false =self true < true`, `floats < true = false`, `strings < true CMP LessThan = true`, `empty = true sizes false`, `nested < true = false`, `PASS` | identical | (walk unchanged) |
| `OpenWhereVarCond` (a condition on the declaration's own `where`-clause variable) | 'E is undefined.' | the same: the name binder refuses it before the checker | |
| `OpenParentCond`, `OpenParentPlain(2)`, `OpenGenericComprisesOrd` (a generic trait that opens a type and overrides an inherited method) | 'F is not in the kind env [E -> ...]' | the same | (NEW-X-3, section 4.4) |
| `ImportList` (a component that imports `List.{...}`), typecheck | 5 errors, 'LexicographicOrder is undefined.' at `List.fsi:67` first | 6 errors, 'ZeroIndexed is undefined.' at `:67` first | (row 71's note, section 4.4) |

No walk value moved: walk's answers on lists are the base's, as the report says.

## 3. Findings

1. **A crash where the base compiled** (defect, fixed, 4.1). With conditional parents read, a subtype question about a type that inherits through a conditional parent asks the condition's type variable for its bound. The code generator's analyzer binds no declaration's static parameters, so `CodeGen`'s check of identically covered inherited methods (`STypesUtil.scala:1563-1570`, from `CodeGen.java:485`) died with a `CompilerBug`, 'E is not in the kind env [][]', for a program the base compiles and runs (`CondInheritGen`). At the switch-over the same question is asked of every object below `List` that inherits `=` from `List` and from `LexicographicOrder`.
2. **An unconditional entry checked under another entry's condition** (defect, fixed, contested, 4.2). `TypeWellFormedChecker` checked the whole `extends` clause with every entry's conditions holding, so `Wrap[\E\]`, well formed only where `E` is ordered, was accepted beside a conditional entry, and the program died at link time where the condition fails (`CondOtherEntry`). P-151 and the curator's reading put the members under the condition, not the other entries; the peers scope a condition to its own conformance.
3. **The refusal test asserted its count only** (correction, 4.3). `XXXCondExtendRefuseChecker` was keyed on 'has 2 errors'; it now also matches the two refused calls.
4. **Specification sentences** (correction, 4.3). The Appendix I entry's Effect named the partial-order departure against `algebraic-constraints.tex` only; the comparisons subsection of the operators chapter ("lists whose elements support these same comparison operators", `Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:293-295`) is false on the checker for lists of `RR64` after the change, though the brief says it holds. The team's own sketch of conditional subtyping (`Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/internal-document.tex:483-512`, "Conditional Subtyping") writes entries under boolean constraints and `where`-clause variables, which the change reads at every instance; the Effect now names both.
5. **Record** (correction, 4.4). Row 71's notes are stale (`ImportList`: 6 errors on the head, `ZeroIndexed` first). A crash measured on the base and the head alike, NEW-X-3, filed as a row. The FACTS entry names my test.
6. **A latent gap, recorded in NEW-X-3's notes.** The opening branch of the trait-type case reads `parents(p)` only (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:306-308`), so a conditional parent of a parent that opens types would be lost even where its condition holds. No program reaches it: every generic trait that opens a type and inherits a method crashes first (NEW-X-3), and a trait with no static parameter cannot state a condition (`OpenWhereVarCond`: 'E is undefined.'). No test can be written for it today.
7. **The failure-mode question.** The change turns the checker's refusals of conditional members into accepted programs that die where the condition fails: on the compiled path with `NoSuchMethodError` at the call (NEW-X-1, `CondMember2`), under walk with 'Cannot find definition for method ...'. My fix 4.1 turns a `CompilerBug` into the base's answer, the parent read at every instance, for an analyzer that binds no variable of the condition. No quiet wrong value comes of either.
8. **My first commit's footer.** `37f5f8c84` ends with the session's generic co-author line, not the skill's (`Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>`); it was pushed, so I left it; every later commit carries the skill's footer.

## 4. The fixes

### 4.1 `24bafdd04`, settled: a condition on an unbound type variable is left unread

`TypeAnalyzer.condition` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:963-975`): a condition `X extends B` whose `X` is a type variable that the analyzer's kind environment does not bind holds; any other condition is `pSub(X, B)` as before. The lookup counts as a read of the context, so no such answer is shared as a ground answer.
